title: Chapter 24 – Judgment at Dawn
html:
[Lin Clan – Lin Jian]

The scrap of paper weighs nothing at all.

Lin Jian holds it in his closed fist at the foot of the dark stairs, an hour before dawn, and cannot get over how little it weighs. A torn corner of flyleaf, folded four times, with a smudge on it the size of a grain of rice. Whatever is in it, the Interface says, is enough to stop a heart. He has carried it up forty steps against his ribs, and through the sleeping yard, and past a sentry who nodded to him as to a ghost, and now he stands in the cold kitchen passage with the weight of a whole house on it.

His mother is waiting by the stove.

She is dressed already, in her plain gray work short robe, with her hair bound tight and the Tidal Spear leaning in the corner by the door. She does not ask where he has been. She looks at his hands, then at his face, and then she holds out her own hand, palm up, and waits.

He puts the paper in it.

She does not unfold it. She closes her fingers on it as a woman closes her fingers on a coin she has been owed for a long time. "The Patriarch will want this before the council begins," she says. "He will not ask where it came from."

"Mother—"

"I did not ask you either." She tucks it into the hidden pocket inside her sleeve. For the first time in many weeks, the corner of her mouth moves. "Go and find a seat behind the screen. Bring Lin Hu. And Jian."

"Yes?"

"Whatever you hear in there, you are a nine-year-old boy who was told to stay out of the way."

"I know."

"Good." She touches his hair once, quickly. "Keep it that way."

* * *

The council hall of the Lin clan was built for forty people and has not seen forty in a generation.

This morning there are thirty-one adults on the benches, and every one of them has dressed as for a funeral. The Patriarch sits at the head of the long table. To his right is Father, upright but pale, with his useless left hand laid against his knee; to his left, Elder Aunt Lin Wenjun, who has been the clan's accountant since before Lin Jian's grandfather's brother died, and who is, for once, not scowling at anybody. Along the walls are the heads of the five side branches, the farmers, the shepherds, and the masons; the Hollow's two oldest hunters; Feng and his cousins in their cadet jackets; Third Aunt Wenqing with her satchel; and, at the far end of the table, in the steward's seat, with his book closed in front of him and both hands flat on the cover, Second Uncle Lin Wenhai.

He does not look up when the doors shut.

Lin Jian watches from behind a folding screen of painted paper that stands at the back of the hall, where the children are put when a matter is too serious to send them away and too grave for them to sit in the room. The panel has a tear in one hinge. Through it he can see the whole table. Beside him, wedged into the corner with his knees drawn up, sits a boy of eleven with his father's long nose and his father's habit of biting his lip. Lin Hu has not spoken since they sat. He has not asked why his father looks as though he has not slept.

On the long table, at the Patriarch's right hand, lies a single yellow slip.

Lin Jian knows it from the workroom. It is Father's, and it is a Yellow Grade talisman: a Greater Contract Witness, drawn in black-and-gold ink, with the clan's seal at one corner and a blank place at the other. "Each person who speaks will press a thumb to the corner," Father told him last night. "It records the words and the voice. It will not lie for you and it will not lie against you. It is simply a witness that cannot be bribed."

The slip begins to glow, softly, the color of candle-flame, as the last of the doors is barred.

Grandfather lifts one hand.

"Under the law of this house," says Lin Zhenshan, "the council sits at the request of any member, on any matter that touches the safety of the hill. I called it. I will not speak first. Where a grievance concerns the body, the law gives the first voice to the one who has tended the body." He turns his head. "Wenqing."

* * *

Third Aunt stands. She sets her satchel on the table and opens it, and does not look at her brother-in-law at the end of the bench.

"On the night we burned my son," she says, "I found a flake of red lacquer in the mourning wine jar that Lin Wenhai had carried to the pyre. A small thing. A chip from the rim of a cup. I put it away in Bo's box of milk teeth, because I did not know what else to do with it." Her voice is perfectly steady. It is the steadiest voice Lin Jian has ever heard. "It is lacquer from the Pavilion of Nine Dice, in Willow Ford. I took it to the Pavilion in the third month. I will not say how."

A murmur. She presses her thumb to the slip, and it brightens.

"Four days ago I examined the Steward's neck. He had complained of a stiffness in the shoulder. I found, below the left ear, a dark scar the size of a fingernail, with three black threads running out of it along the meridian. They had gone dead. A thing had been seated there that fed on his Qi, and it was cut loose this winter." She turns, finally, and meets Wenhai's eyes across the table. "Blood Shadow work, Second Brother. I have seen the like twice in my life. In both cases the patient had been told what he must do, or the thing would be woken."

Silence. In the stillness, Lin Jian hears Lin Hu stop breathing.

Wenhai's hands have not moved. He is looking at the book on the table, as if it might open and tell him what to say.

"I have nothing more," says Wenqing, and sits. Only the knuckles of her right hand, white on the bench beside her, say what it has cost.

* * *

His mother stands next.

She does it without ceremony, with a bundle of papers under her arm and a leather bag at her waist. She walks the length of the room and lays the papers down on the table in front of the Patriarch. They are the six nights' work, the reconstruction Lin Jian made in lamplight over the winter, copied out in her own square hand and signed in her own name.

"Five hundred and twelve low-grade stones," says Su Qinghe. "Over eleven years. Not taken in one theft. Taken in forty small ones, here a basket, there a sack, entered in the book as spoilage, wastage, a bad season. The Steward kept the book, and so the book never complained." Her voice is level, as flat as a blade. "I found the pattern. I will not say how."

Elder Aunt Wenjun is already bending over the sheet, her spectacles halfway down her nose. Her lips are moving. She comes to the bottom of the page, and her mouth tightens, and she whispers something that sounds like forty-one, forty-two, and looks up.

"It is correct," she says.

"Old Fang," says Grandfather.

The counter shuffles forward, a bent little man with his tally sticks tied in a bundle on his back. He lays them on the table in a neat row. They are cut from willow and split down the middle, one half for the buyer and one for the seller, notched in the old manner. "These are the sticks for the last three harvest tolls at Willow Ford," he says. "My half. The Steward's half is in his book. They do not match." He points. "Here. And here. Where he cut a notch one notch shorter in the book than on the stick."

"How can you be sure?" a mason asks.

"Because I made them," says Old Fang, with great dignity. "And because the notches on the book's halves are cut with a knife that is not mine. A crooked knife, a left-handed knife. I have never seen a left-handed man in Willow Ford who does the books." He looks up. "Except one."

Lin Jian remembers the sticks. He remembers the faint blue shimmer when he scanned them, the 99.1 percent match on the true halves and the cold gap where the others should have been. Left-handed. He had not noticed that.

And behind him, very softly, he hears Lin Hu whisper, "My father writes with his left."

"I know," says Lin Jian, and does not look at him.

Father rises next. He is unsteady on his feet, and carries a small stack of paper-bound books under his good arm, and he sets them on the table one by one. Twelve of them, thin and well-thumbed. "These I found in a locked drawer in the steward's room," he says. "I had gone to look for a brush I lent him. They are copybooks. Someone has been practicing a hand."

"Whose?" says Grandfather.

"Yours, Father."

A sound goes through the room like wind in dry grass.

"The seal-hand," Wenyuan says. "Your signature, your characters for granted and approved and Lin Zhenshan, by his own brush. Twelve books. A month's labor each. By the last, it is nearly perfect." He sets down the last. "Whoever wrote these meant to write a second document, one day, in a hand that no one would doubt."

The silence is absolute.

"Old Hu," says Grandfather.

* * *

The refiner comes in last, from the back, leaning on his rod.

He walks the whole length of the hall, and nobody speaks. When he reaches the table he does not bow. He puts a canvas-wrapped bundle down in front of the Patriarch with the stump of his left arm and unwraps it with his one hand. Out of the cloth comes a small bag of oilcloth, double-waxed, and a blue-bound ledger, and a letter folded in thirds.

"From the old kiln on the lower terrace," says Hu. "North wall. Four loose bricks. I took them out an hour before sunrise." His eye goes, for the briefest instant, to the screen. "I was told where to look."

Grandfather opens the bag. Silver tumbles out, a heap of low-grade stones, and three heavier ones, each the color of a pale moon, that roll away across the wood and come to rest against the ledger. Elder Aunt Wenjun counts under her breath. "Two hundred and eleven," she says. "And three of middle grade."

He unfolds the letter. For a moment he reads it in silence. Then he lifts it, so that all the benches can see the red wax: a jagged ridge beneath a rising sun.

"The crest of Red Ridge," he says. "Addressed to the Steward of Green Pine Hill."

He reads it aloud, every word, in his dry old voice, to the end: whatever its outcome, the hill will need a master who values good neighbors. When he has finished, no one moves, because no one needs to.

"There is one more matter," says the Patriarch.

Su Qinghe steps up to the table. She lays something in his hand. Lin Jian sees her do it, quick and plain, a small folded corner of paper passed from one palm to another as a woman might pass a pin. Grandfather does not look at it. He turns toward the end of the table. He opens the paper on the wood in front of Wenhai, and lets everyone see the smudge, a fleck of gray-white no larger than a seed.

"Yesterday, the Steward opened the jade box. In the sight of this family. Do you remember that, Wenhai?" His voice is almost kind. "I remember that I tested the pill with a silver needle, last night, before I locked the chamber. I am an old man, and old men are suspicious. The needle went black. I scraped what I found from the surface." He touches the paper. "The Sect names it Heart-Withering Dust. It is tasteless. It is odorless. It is harmless to a man who sits still. In a man who draws in the Qi of a breakthrough, it stills the heart for the space of one breath, and the foundation breaks."

Nobody looks at the boy behind the screen. Nobody has any reason to.

"Where did you get it, Wenhai?" says Grandfather.

For a long moment Wenhai says nothing. He sits with both hands on the cover of his book. And then, as the slip on the table gives its soft glow, he lifts his head, and Lin Jian, who has braced for a lie, sees instead the face of a man who has been drowning for eleven years and has just been told he may breathe.

"I will tell you," he says. "I will tell you all of it."

* * *

The Contract Witness records every word.

Lin Jian does not need it. He will remember the next quarter hour for the rest of his life.

Wenhai speaks in a low, dry voice, with his hands on the book and his eyes on the grain of the wood. Eleven years ago, he says, he was twenty-six, newly made steward of the hill, and a fool. He had a talent for numbers and a weakness for dice. The Pavilion of Nine Dice in Willow Ford gave him credit when he was winning, and gave him more when he began to lose. In two years he owed four hundred stones.

"And one night a man bought my debt," he says. "All of it, in one evening, for half its face. A man in a gray-green robe, who did not give his name. He said I need not pay. He said the Zhao family would be glad of a friend in the steward's seat. He said it would cost me only a little."

The small, early things, he says. A word about the patrol. A date for the harvest toll. A copy of the old ledger. Each one seemed too small to matter.

"I took it as a loan," he says. "It was a leash."

This past winter, he says, the council sent a party to Salt Hollow for ink-blood: Mao to lead, Feng, Shu, and Bo. He wrote the plan down himself, in his own neat hand, because that was his office. The route, the day, the number of men. He passed it on the next night, at the old shrine, in the dark. He did not think of it as a killing. He thought of it as a favor.

At the far end of the bench, Third Aunt Wenqing does not move.

"Bo died in the hollow," says Wenhai. His voice does not rise. It simply stops being a voice and becomes a sound. "And the man who did it came to me afterward, in the dark, and put Bo's belt in my hands. He said: You will want to see what it costs when you stop. Gu Yan. That was the name. The Vulture. He put a thing in my neck, a blood seed, he called it, and said if I ever spoke, he would wake it. It woke twice. Both times I wished I were dead."

Something moves behind the screen. Lin Hu has put his hand over his own mouth.

"He is dead now, I am told," says Wenhai. He closes his eyes. "I felt the seed die, in the second month. It was the first breath I had drawn freely in a year. And I still did not tell you, because the Zhao had not died with him."

He opens his eyes.

"They told me to touch the pill," he says. "I touched it. Wenqing. I am sorry. I am sorry for all of it. I have no excuse that does not shame me worse."

Nobody answers him. Beyond the screen, Lin Jian can hear his own pulse in his ears. Wenqing rises from the bench. She looks at the man at the end of the table for a long moment. Then she says, quite quietly, "I would have forgiven the dice," and sits down again, and does not speak after that.

At last Grandfather says, very quietly, "Wenhai. Under the law of this house, a man who is proved to have sold his family stands before the council and is judged. You know the sentences."

"I know them."

"Do you wish to say anything to the council before it votes?"

"Only one thing." Wenhai turns his head, and for a moment his gaze finds the torn hinge of the screen, and the boy behind it, and Lin Jian knows that he has seen. "Do not let them take it out on Hu."

And then he moves.

* * *

It is very fast. Lin Jian has never seen a Qi Gatherer move so fast, and he has seen Feng.

Wenhai's right hand goes to his belt. A slip of yellow paper comes out of nowhere and cracks between his fingers, and a wave of wind goes through the hall like a slap. The benches rock. Candles gutter. Elder Aunt Wenjun's papers go up in a white storm, and the whole room rises to its feet, shouting, as the Steward of Green Pine Hill turns and runs straight at the east window.

Gale Sprint. Lin Jian knows the slip by the howl of it. It is a Yellow Grade talisman, a sprint charm, the sort a messenger might carry on a long road. It is one of Father's. He took it from the workroom. Of course he did. It was on the long table all week.

"Stop him!" shouts a mason.

Feng is already moving, spear in hand, and two of the older hunters, and Mother, who has a hand on the Tidal Spear and a face like stone.

"No!"

The voice does not rise. It does not need to. It falls across the hall like a stone dropped in a well, and everyone stops.

Grandfather has not left his chair.

Wenhai goes out through the window in a spray of paper shutters. There is a clatter of boots on the sill, a thud in the yard, the long dwindling sound of a man running faster than any man should run, and then nothing but a pale dust drifting down from the sill, and the sound of thirty-one people breathing.

"Sit down," says Lin Zhenshan.

They sit.

"He will not be followed," the old man says. He looks tired. He looks a thousand years old. "Not by anyone. That is the judgment of the Patriarch, and I will answer for it. He will carry to Zhao Heng the one thing he has left to give, which is the date of the attempt. And Zhao Heng will believe it, because it comes from his own man." A pause. "Midsummer. Twenty-nine days. If the Zhao want to come into this house, they will come on the longest day, by the book, on ground we have prepared. I would rather meet them there than anywhere else."

Su Qinghe is looking at him. Lin Jian sees the understanding move across her face, like a hand wiping a table.

"This council is adjourned," says Grandfather. "Qinghe, Wenqing, Wenyuan, stay."

* * *

By noon, he has worked it out.

He had set it the night before, almost without thinking, on the high ridge above the east wall. A tiny slip of yellow paper that Father gave him, folded around a stone and weighed down in the long grass, with a thread of his own Qi laid across the ground like a hair across a page. He felt it flare only once, a hot, bright hiss against the inside of his thumb, at the moment that Wenhai went over the wall.

Lin Jian sits in the grass above the east wall with the sun on his back and thinks about it.

The pins did not sing.

Six of them, along the length of that wall, every one sunk by his own hands to the hilt, every one tuned to the anchor plate in the chamber below. Six pins that should have shrieked at the first stranger's boot. They stayed silent. He tested them this morning. There is nothing wrong with them. They simply did not fire.

Someone lifted the linking rune.

There is only one person who could. Only one person who has the plate in his hand every night, and the key.

"I saw him," says a voice.

Feng is sitting on the wall below with his spear across his knees, looking out over the valley. He does not turn his head. "Last night, late. Grandfather was out on the wall by himself, with his hand on the anchor plate. He did something with his thumb, a small thing, and went in again." He shrugs. "I assumed it was repairs."

"It was not."

"No." Feng looks at him, finally, from under his brows. "He wanted Wenhai to run."

"He wanted Wenhai to carry something."

"The date. Midsummer. The day Zhao comes." Feng's jaw is tight. "He let a traitor go over our wall to tell the enemy exactly when and where to attack, because it means the enemy comes when we are ready." He lets out a breath. "I could not have done it, Jian. I would have wanted to put a spear through him."

"I know."

"You do not seem surprised."

"I am nine," says Lin Jian, and Feng gives a shaky snort of a laugh, and the two of them sit there in the sun and say nothing more.

* * *

Lin Hu is still in the corner behind the screen when he comes back.

The hall is empty. The benches are pushed crooked. Someone has opened the shutters, and a long beam of sunlight lies on the table where the Contract Witness slip has gone gray and dead, a sheet of paper no more than that. The boy sits with his knees drawn up and his face on his arms.

Lin Jian sits down beside him.

He does not say that it will be all right. He is not a fool. He does not say that his uncle is not a bad man, because the man is a traitor and a killer's tool and has also been, for eleven years, a father who tied the shoes of his son. He sits. He waits. After a long time Lin Hu says, in a very small voice, "Will they hurt me?"

"No."

"My mother."

"No."

"How do you know?"

"Because my mother is standing in the door," says Lin Jian.

She is. She has been there for a minute, he thinks. She comes in without a word, and kneels in front of the older boy with her hands on her knees, and looks at him for a long time with her plain, tired, watchful face. Then she says, in the voice she uses for the weather, "Hu. Get up. You are coming to eat."

"But—"

"You are a Lin," says Su Qinghe. "In this house, that means you eat." She holds out her hand. After a moment the boy takes it, and she pulls him to his feet, and walks him out of the hall with his hand in hers.

At the door she glances back. It is a very brief look, and Lin Jian cannot read it, except that it is not a question.

* * *

Evening finds him in the forge, where the fire is low and Old Hu is asleep with his chin on his chest.

Third Aunt Wenqing is there too, cross-legged on the floor with her satchel open, and between them on the anvil sit three pale stones.

Mid-grade. Each is the size of a hen's egg and glows with a faint, cool light, like a bead of moonlight left in a bowl. Grandfather brought them down himself an hour ago, and laid them on the anvil, and said only: "Three. For three pills. For the man who needs his sword arm back before the longest day." He did not say whose. He did not need to. He looked at Wenqing, and then at the old refiner, and then, for a very long moment, at Lin Jian. "Help them," he said. "Hu is getting slow in his old age."

Then he went back up the hill, and asked nothing at all.

Wenqing has not touched the stones. She is looking at them as one looks at a very large sum of money. "Hu says it is a formula he remembers," she says. "I have said nothing to Wenyuan. If the first pill fails, I would rather he did not know there was a first pill." She turns her head. "You will tell me if I am being foolish."

"Third Aunt," says Lin Jian. "May I?"

She nods.

He picks up the first stone.

It is warm. He expected it to be cold. It fills his palm with a slow, even pulse, and the sense that something very large has been patiently folded into something very small.

```
[Scan — Mid-Grade Spirit Stone]
Qi density: 100x low-grade
Purity: 94%
Capacity: sufficient to run one Green Pulse variant pill-cycle
Novel material: first reading of this class
CE: +8 (total: 131 / 400)
```

Beneath the numbers the Interface flickers, then offers, as it does when he is not looking for it, a second line.

```
[Estimate — Lin Wenyuan, damaged channels]
Three pills (variant formula, 1 stone each)
Projected restoration: 38–52% of torn channels
Time to completion: 29 days at current rate
```

Twenty-nine days. The same number. It is no coincidence. Everything in this house is running down toward a single day, and he has a month to make it come out right.

Lin Jian closes his fingers around the stone. It is the first moment in many weeks that he has not been afraid.

"Third Aunt," he says. "Tell me exactly what the fern does to a torn channel."
